title: A Prescriptive Learning Analytics Framework: Beyond Predictive Modelling and onto Explainable AI with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in learning analytics research: most work predicts which students are at risk, but does not explain those predictions clearly or translate them into actionable, individualized advice. The author argues that predictive systems in higher education need to move beyond black-box risk classification toward explainable and prescriptive analytics that stakeholders can understand and use. The paper is not a secondary-school writing-feedback study and does not provide direct evidence about ChatGPT-generated formative feedback on student drafts.

The paper proposes a Prescriptive Learning Analytics Framework (PLAF) that combines predictive modelling, explainable AI tools, counterfactual analysis, and ChatGPT. The framework includes steps for data preparation, feature engineering, predictive model training, global model interpretability, local explanation of individual predictions, counterfactual modelling to identify feasible behavior changes, and conversion of those counterfactual outputs into human-readable advice using ChatGPT. The empirical component demonstrates predictive modelling of programme completion/non-completion using institutional data, with CatBoost performing best among several machine learning models; SHAP and Anchors are used to explain predictions, and DiCE is used to generate prescriptive suggestions.

The population consists of undergraduate students at a single Australasian higher education institution, using data from 2018 to 2022 drawn from student management and Moodle systems. The context is higher education retention and programme completion, not classroom writing instruction. Stakeholders discussed include students/learners, educators/instructors, and academic advisors or support teams. The ChatGPT use is limited to translating analytics-derived prescriptive recommendations into natural language, rather than interacting directly with students’ authored text.

The main conclusion is that a unified framework can connect prediction, explanation, and prescriptive support in learning analytics, potentially making risk predictions more transparent, trustworthy, and actionable. The paper concludes that current learning analytics research underuses explainability and prescriptive methods, and that large language models such as ChatGPT may help render analytics outputs into accessible feedback. However, the work does not test instructional effects of ChatGPT feedback against teacher or peer feedback, so it should be excluded from direct-evidence syntheses on AI draft feedback in grades 9–12.
quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a predictive modeling and framework paper with cross-validation on observational higher-education data, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of an educational intervention. It provides quantitative model performance evidence but no causal estimate of intervention impact on learners.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful institutional impact through accurate risk prediction, but actual downstream effects of the intervention framework on student outcomes are not measured. Impact is therefore promising but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Machine-learning early warning system predicting higher-education programme non-completion from student management and LMS data, with explainable AI and counterfactual prescriptive recommendations for at-risk learners.

ChatGPT is used to translate counterfactual prescriptive analytics outputs into human-readable natural-language advice for at-risk students; it is not evaluated as a writing-feedback tool on student drafts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports strong predictive performance for identifying higher-education students at risk of programme non-completion using institutional and LMS data. Across 14,918 student-year data points from one Australasian HEI, CatBoost achieved F1=94.5% (SD 0.6), accuracy=92.0% (SD 0.7), AUC=88.3% (SD 0.6), recall=96.7% (SD 0.7), and precision=92.5% (SD 0.7), outperforming baseline models; however, no causal intervention effect on retention or completion is tested.
finding.measure: Programme/qualiﬁcation completion prediction performance (F1, accuracy, AUC, recall, precision)
finding.study_size: n=14,918 data points; 7,108 students implied by 3,693 completers and 3,415 non-completers
finding.std_deviation: F1 SD=0.6; Accuracy SD=0.7; AUC SD=0.6; Recall SD=0.7; Precision SD=0.7
